A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same dispersion research. Text, equations, figures, tables, and all proof and experimental appendices are readable and support a reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original Tammes and synthetic embedding experiments, ImageNet-200 classification results, and discrete and continuous-output machine translation results.

after.justification: v2 reports original dispersion, classification, and translation experiments, including revised synthetic evaluations and new timing measurements.

M1.justification: The proposed Lloyd and Sliced objectives, circular sorting/projection procedure, and Sliced gradient are retained. MMD is relabeled MHE with an RBF kernel. Axis-aligned slicing, explained more fully in v2, was already used in v1 Section 4.2.

E1.justification: v2 Section 4.2 adds uniformly initialized synthetic embeddings alongside the retained power-spherical initialization with concentration 100. v1 evaluated only the latter condition. ImageNet-200, both WMT language pairs, and continuous-output translation retain their dataset and task coverage.

E2.justification: v2 Figures 4–5 add Laplace-kernel comparators and expand the kernel/distance variants evaluated within MHE. The downstream comparator sets remain unchanged after matching MMD to MHE with RBF, MMA to geodesic MM, and MMCS to squared-Euclidean MM. This extends an existing comparison family.

E3.justification: Tammes optimization changes from 2.5k to 10k iterations, with RBF gamma changing from 25 to 1 and Riesz s from 0 to 1. Synthetic dimensionality changes from 128 to 64, with computation-matched batching: MHE/MMA batches change from 16K to 512 and Lloyd samples from 8192 to 512. The additional Tammes configurations with 13, 14, and 128 points are removed.

E4.justification: v2 adds a kernel-gradient analysis showing how interactions vary with angle (Figure 2), and examines sensitivity to clumped versus uniform initialization (Figure 5). The Sliced estimator-convergence study and translation gradient diagnostics are retained; expanded explanation of the former does not establish a new experiment.

E5.justification: v2 Figure 5 explicitly reports means and standard errors over three random initializations; v1 Figure 3 gives no corresponding run-count or uncertainty specification. The new timing table also reports means and standard errors. These disclosures do not establish that repeated-run counts increased.

E6.justification: Tammes and synthetic results are substantially replaced under changed settings. RBF/MMD is near MM/KoLeo in v1 Figure 2 but performs substantially worse in v2 Figure 4. v2 adds timing and uniform-initialization results and removes the extra Tammes result panels. The CoNMT Euclidean baseline BLEU changes from 27.8 to 29.0 (v1 Table 3; v2 Table 4). Classification accuracies and discrete NMT scores are retained.

T1.justification: v2 adds an MMD-estimation proposition, extends the MM/KoLeo inequality, and introduces limit derivations connecting kernel energies to Tammes optimization in Appendix A.1.1. It also corrects the spherical-variance expression to use the norm of the mean. Existing MMD invariance and Sliced proofs largely remain, including the circular-dispersion lemma moved into the main text. Some new statements contain mathematical inconsistencies.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: connecting dispersion objectives through MMD, proposing Lloyd and Sliced regularizers, evaluating vision and language applications, and investigating Riemannian optimization. Rewritten contribution wording does not materially change these claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive qualifications about KoLeo on lower-dimensional manifolds, geodesic kernel positive definiteness, finite-configuration MMD, and difficulties with alternative variance objectives. Its revised synthetic interpretation recommends Sliced for initially poor dispersion and MM objectives once points are already separated. This substantially expands applicability guidance beyond v1's aggregate rankings and general dispersion/performance tradeoff.

D1.justification: v1 supplies an implementation URL and states that the code is available; v2 replaces this with a future open-source release promise. Conversely, v2 newly documents decoder embedding tying, regularizer sampling, frozen CoNMT embeddings, offline optimization settings including 500 epochs and MHE batch size 2000, and the configuration used for Sliced estimator convergence. These materially change the available reproducibility information.

R1.justification: v2 adds targeted literature on spherical embeddings, geodesic kernels, manifold entropy estimation, and classical Riemannian optimization, including Feragen et al. and Nilsson and Kleijn. Several generic entropy-regularization references are removed. These additions refine the mathematical positioning while retaining the same central relationship to prior dispersion methods.

P1.justification: Large portions of the background, method explanations, and experimental narrative are rewritten. Riemannian optimization moves from Section 3.4 into the background, CoNMT becomes Section 4.5, contribution bullets become prose, and terminology and notation are standardized. Appendices are reorganized and explanations substantially expanded.

P2.justification: v2 adds geometry and kernel-gradient figures plus timing and kernel tables. It redraws the Sliced illustration and Tammes plots, expands the synthetic display from two panels to four, and removes the additional Tammes figure. Existing tables and diagnostic figures are also resized or relocated, substantially changing the visual presentation.

improvement.justification: v2 improves empirical assessment through computation-matched synthetic comparisons, explicit uncertainty reporting, and fuller implementation explanations. However, the available-code statement becomes a future-release promise, and new mathematical statements introduce errors: Proposition 1 omits the constant required by Lemma 1, while the added first inequality in Equation 5 reverses the comparison implied by the definitions. These gains and regressions in reproducibility and mathematical reliability prevent a confident net quality judgment.
